transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… it’s probably not a huge thing, but I’ve noticed I have trouble just staying seated when I’m supposed to. Like in staff meetings, or even at dinner, everyone else is sitting and I’ll suddenly get up to refill coffee, check a handout, or walk to the back of the room. It feels like there’s a reason in the moment, but honestly, it’s not usually urgent. I just… don’t seem to sit still as easily as other people do, if that makes sense.
When you get up like that, does it feel like you have to do it to relieve an uncomfortable urge?

I don’t know if I’d call it an uncomfortable urge exactly… that sounds a bit dramatic, maybe. It’s more like, in the moment, getting up feels like the natural thing to do—refill my coffee, look at a handout, go to the back of the room. But if I’m honest, it’s usually not really urgent. I just seem to end up out of my seat when everyone else is still sitting. Does that make sense?
Do these times when you can’t stay seated happen mainly during periods when your mood is unusually high or energized?

I don’t think I’ve noticed it being tied to a particularly high mood, no. It’s more just… in ordinary situations, like staff meetings or dinner, I’ll suddenly be up to refill coffee or check a handout or walk to the back, even when it isn’t really necessary. It’s not like I feel wildly energized, at least not that I can tell.
When you’re sitting there, do you feel anxious?

Not really… I mean, not in a big way. I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there worrying or feeling panicky. It’s more just that I notice myself wanting to move or getting up before I’ve really thought it through. Unless that counts as anxiety? I don’t think it does, but I’m not completely sure.
Did you have this same trouble staying seated when you were a child?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I was a good student, so I don’t want to make it sound like I was always in trouble, but my report cards did say things like I was bright but had trouble staying in my seat or waiting my turn.

And my mother used to tease me that before I was ten I’d practically worn a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener. So yes, I suppose it goes back quite a long way.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on a task or what someone is saying?

I’m not sure how to answer that, exactly. I mean, I can usually manage, especially at work, because I know I’m expected to listen and keep things moving properly. But yes, I do sometimes realize I’ve drifted a bit when someone is talking, or I have to pull myself back to the task.

I wouldn’t want to overstate it, though. It’s not as if I can’t function—at least I don’t think so. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do these problems with sitting still or staying focused cause trouble for you at work, at home, or in relationships?

A little, yes… though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. I think it has started to affect things with people, especially at work or in community things like my book club.

In meetings, I can tell people lose patience with me if I’m restless or if I’m not quite tracking the way I should. And at book club sometimes I leave feeling embarrassed, like I haven’t really connected properly with everyone. I don’t think anyone is being unkind, exactly, but I do notice it. Is that the sort of trouble you mean?
Do you notice this same restlessness and drifting off in more than one setting, like both at work and at home?

Yes, I think it does show up in more than one place. Not constantly, but enough that I’ve noticed it.

At work, in meetings, I’ll find myself getting up to refill coffee or check a handout, or I’ll walk to the back of the room as if there’s something I need to do. And at home, even at dinner, I’ll pop up for something that probably could have waited.

It’s a bit embarrassing to say, because it’s not usually urgent. I just feel like I need to move, and I make it look useful, if that makes sense.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

I don’t think so, not in a big way. I mean, I worry about normal things—work, family, whether I’ve said the right thing—but I wouldn’t say I’m worrying all the time for no reason.

Unless I’m misunderstanding what you mean by “a lot”? I don’t want to give the wrong impression.
